text:
Scrap the Parking Minimums

Somewhere in your city's zoning code there is a table that says how many parking spaces a bowling alley needs per lane, how many a funeral home needs per seat, and how many a one-bedroom apartment needs regardless of who lives in it. These numbers look like engineering. They are closer to folklore. Most were copied from neighbouring towns or from surveys of suburban sites with free parking and no transit, then frozen into law decades ago. Cities should delete them.

Removing minimum parking requirements does not ban parking. It means the person building the apartment block, the shop or the clinic decides how much parking to provide, based on what tenants and customers will actually pay for, rather than a planner's table deciding for them. That distinction matters, because the debate is usually framed as cars versus no cars. It is really a question of who is better placed to guess demand for a particular site: the people risking money on it, or a ratio written in 1975.

Start with cost. A surface parking space consumes roughly 300 square feet once you count the aisles. A space in a structured garage commonly costs tens of thousands of dollars to build, and underground spaces cost more still. Those costs do not vanish. They are folded into rents, into the price of a meal, into the cost of a new home. A renter who owns no car pays for a space anyway, bundled invisibly into the lease. Since car ownership rises with income, the mandate works as a transfer from poorer households to richer ones, enforced by the planning department.

Then there is what never gets built. Parking minimums quietly kill projects that would otherwise make sense. A small apartment building on a narrow city lot often cannot physically fit the required spaces, so the lot stays a lot. An old shopfront cannot become a restaurant because the change of use triggers a parking requirement the site cannot meet, so it stays empty. The older, walkable neighbourhoods that people pay a premium to live in are, in most cities, illegal to build today, largely because of parking rules. We have outlawed the places we like best.

The requirements also produce far more parking than anyone uses. Studies of American cities have repeatedly found that parking lots sit substantially empty even at peak hours, because the ratios are calibrated to the busiest day of the year at a site with no alternative to driving. The result is the familiar landscape of the retail strip: buildings stranded in asphalt, too far apart to walk between, which guarantees that everyone drives, which appears to justify the asphalt. The rule manufactures the demand it claims to be measuring.

That land has other uses. It could hold homes in cities desperately short of them. It could hold businesses that pay property tax; a parking lot generates a fraction of the revenue per acre that a modest building does, while requiring the same roads and pipes to reach it. It could hold trees instead of a surface that sheds stormwater and radiates heat.

The evidence from cities that have acted is encouraging. Buffalo removed minimums citywide in 2017, and subsequent research found that many new mixed-use projects built less parking than the old code would have forced, while developers still provided parking where they judged it necessary. Minneapolis, which eliminated minimums as part of a broader package of reforms, saw strong housing construction and rents that rose more slowly than in comparable cities. Parking was only one piece of that package, and I would not claim it deserves all the credit, but nothing in the record suggests it did harm. In none of these places did parking disappear. Lenders and tenants still demand it. Developers simply stopped building the spaces nobody wanted.

The strongest objection is spillover. If a new building has too little parking, residents will park on neighbouring streets, and the people already there will bear the cost. This is a real concern, and it deserves a real answer rather than dismissal. But the answer is to manage the kerb, not to mandate garages. Residential permit schemes, time limits and metered pricing address spillover directly, at the place where it occurs. Requiring every building in the city to overbuild parking in order to protect free street parking in a few contested blocks is an enormously expensive way to solve a problem that a permit and a meter solve cheaply.

A second objection is that some people need cars: the disabled, tradespeople, families in places with poor transit. True, and nothing here stops parking being built for them. Accessible parking requirements can and should remain. In car-dependent suburbs, developers will keep building plenty of parking because their customers will not come otherwise. Reform bites only where the mandate exceeds real demand, which is exactly where it should.

Minimum parking requirements are a rule that raises housing costs, wastes land, entrenches car dependence and rests on numbers nobody can defend. Cities do not need to study them further. They need to strike them out.
